claim: PAM is present in Chlamydomonas and mammalian cilia.
source: We recently identified peptidylglycine α-amidating monooxygenase (PAM), an enzyme required for generating amidated bioactive signaling peptides, in Chlamydomonas and mammalian cilia.
evidence: This statement is presented in the abstract as a finding from recent research by the authors.

claim: PAM is required for normal assembly of motile and primary cilia in Chlamydomonas, planaria and mice.
source: Here, we show that PAM is required for the normal assembly of motile and primary cilia in Chlamydomonas, planaria and mice.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines failed to assemble cilia beyond the transition zone.
source: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines failed to assemble cilia beyond the transition zone, had abnormal Golgi architecture and altered levels of cilia assembly components.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines had abnormal Golgi architecture.
source: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines failed to assemble cilia beyond the transition zone, had abnormal Golgi architecture and altered levels of cilia assembly components.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines had altered levels of cilia assembly components.
source: Chlamydomonas PAM knockdown lines failed to assemble cilia beyond the transition zone, had abnormal Golgi architecture and altered levels of cilia assembly components.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by western blot data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Decreased PAM gene expression reduced motile ciliary density on the ventral surface of planaria.
source: Decreased PAM gene expression reduced motile ciliary density on the ventral surface of planaria and resulted in the appearance of cytosolic axonemes lacking a ciliary membrane.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by scanning electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Decreased PAM gene expression in planaria resulted in the appearance of cytosolic axonemes lacking a ciliary membrane.
source: Decreased PAM gene expression reduced motile ciliary density on the ventral surface of planaria and resulted in the appearance of cytosolic axonemes lacking a ciliary membrane.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 5H-K.

claim: The architecture of primary cilia on neuroepithelial cells in Pam-/- mouse embryos was aberrant.
source: The architecture of primary cilia on neuroepithelial cells in Pam-/- mouse embryos was also aberrant.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PAM activity and alterations in post-Golgi trafficking contribute to the observed ciliogenesis defects.
source: Our data suggest that PAM activity and alterations in post-Golgi trafficking contribute to the observed ciliogenesis defects and provide an unanticipated, highly conserved link between PAM, amidation and ciliary assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data presented throughout the manuscript, including enzyme inhibitor studies and trafficking protein analyses.

claim: There is a highly conserved link between PAM, amidation and ciliary assembly.
source: Our data suggest that PAM activity and alterations in post-Golgi trafficking contribute to the observed ciliogenesis defects and provide an unanticipated, highly conserved link between PAM, amidation and ciliary assembly.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation of similar PAM-related ciliogenesis defects across multiple evolutionarily distant organisms.

claim: Cilia were present in the last common ancestor of eukaryotes.
source: Cilia are ancient microtubule-based organelles derived from the basal body, and were present in the last common ancestor of eukaryotes (Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Carvalho-Santos et al., 2011.

claim: More than 700 proteins are enriched in the cilium.
source: The protein and lipid complements of the cilium are distinct from the rest of the cell; more than 700 proteins and specific lipids such as sterols are enriched in this intricate structure.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ciliary composition.

claim: Specific lipids such as sterols are enriched in the cilium.
source: The protein and lipid complements of the cilium are distinct from the rest of the cell; more than 700 proteins and specific lipids such as sterols are enriched in this intricate structure.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ciliary composition.

claim: Disruption of ciliogenesis or ciliary function leads to ciliopathies.
source: Disruption of ciliogenesis or ciliary function leads to ciliopathies, a group of multisystemic diseases that have partially overlapping, often severe phenotypes, highlighting the importance of understanding these processes in different cells (Brown and Witman, 2014; Fliegauf et al., 2007; Waters and Beales, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Disruption of the secretory pathway by brefeldin A inhibits ciliogenesis.
source: The growing cilium also relies on the delivery of membrane vesicles and proteins derived from the Golgi, and disruption of the secretory pathway by brefeldin A inhibits ciliogenesis (Dentler, 2013; Haller and Fabry, 1998).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dentler, 2013 and Haller and Fabry, 1998.

claim: PAM catalyzes one of the final steps in the biosynthesis of many signaling peptides.
source: Peptidylglycine α-amidating monooxygenase (PAM), a secretory pathway-localized enzyme, catalyzes one of the final steps in the biosynthesis of many signaling peptides (Kumar et al., 2016a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016a.

claim: PAM-catalyzed C-terminal amidation confers bioactivity to secreted peptides such as oxytocin, vasopressin and neuropeptide Y.
source: PAM-catalyzed C-terminal amidation confers bioactivity to secreted peptides such as oxytocin, vasopressin and neuropeptide Y.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PAM function.

claim: The two enzymatic domains of PAM act sequentially on glycine-extended peptide precursors.
source: The two enzymatic domains of PAM act sequentially on glycine-extended peptide precursors.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PAM enzymatic mechanism.

claim: PHM catalyzes the copper and ascorbate dependent hydroxylation of the α-carbon of the terminal glycine.
source: Peptidylglycine α-hydroxylating monooxygenase (PHM) catalyzes the copper and ascorbate dependent hydroxylation of the α-carbon of the terminal glycine, and peptidyl-α-hydroxyglycine α-amidating lyase (PAL) cleaves the N-C bond, generating glyoxylate and the α-amidated peptide.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PHM enzymatic mechanism.

claim: PAL cleaves the N-C bond, generating glyoxylate and the α-amidated peptide.
source: Peptidylglycine α-hydroxylating monooxygenase (PHM) catalyzes the copper and ascorbate dependent hydroxylation of the α-carbon of the terminal glycine, and peptidyl-α-hydroxyglycine α-amidating lyase (PAL) cleaves the N-C bond, generating glyoxylate and the α-amidated peptide.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PAL enzymatic mechanism.

claim: PAM is a type I integral membrane protein containing a cytosolic domain.
source: PAM is a type I integral membrane protein containing a cytosolic domain that is not essential for catalytic activity, but is necessary for routing the enzyme through the secretory and endocytic pathways (Milgram et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Milgram et al., 1993.

claim: The cytosolic domain of PAM is not essential for catalytic activity.
source: PAM is a type I integral membrane protein containing a cytosolic domain that is not essential for catalytic activity, but is necessary for routing the enzyme through the secretory and endocytic pathways (Milgram et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Milgram et al., 1993.

claim: The cytosolic domain of PAM is necessary for routing the enzyme through the secretory and endocytic pathways.
source: PAM is a type I integral membrane protein containing a cytosolic domain that is not essential for catalytic activity, but is necessary for routing the enzyme through the secretory and endocytic pathways (Milgram et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Milgram et al., 1993.

claim: Active PAM enzyme is present in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Based on a phylogenetic study identifying PAM-like genes in green algal genomes, we recently demonstrated the presence of active enzyme in the unicellular eukaryote, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Attenborough et al., 2012; Kumar et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Attenborough et al., 2012 and Kumar et al., 2016b.

claim: The biochemical properties of C. reinhardtii PAM are remarkably similar to those of rat PAM.
source: Despite the evolutionary distance between green algae and mammals, the biochemical properties of C. reinhardtii PAM (CrPAM) are remarkably similar to those of rat PAM.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on experimental characterization.

claim: In both C. reinhardtii and rat, the full-length PAM enzyme is membrane tethered.
source: In both species, the full-length enzyme is membrane tethered, with its two catalytic domains, PHM and PAL, residing in the secretory pathway lumen.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural organization of PAM in both species.

claim: The two catalytic domains of PAM, PHM and PAL, reside in the secretory pathway lumen.
source: In both species, the full-length enzyme is membrane tethered, with its two catalytic domains, PHM and PAL, residing in the secretory pathway lumen.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural organization of PAM.

claim: The catalytic domains of CrPAM can be separated from its transmembrane and cytosolic domains, leading to the generation of soluble bifunctional enzyme that can be secreted from cells.
source: We also demonstrated that the catalytic domains of CrPAM can be separated from its transmembrane and cytosolic domains, leading to the generation of soluble bifunctional enzyme that can be secreted from cells (Kumar et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016b.

claim: PAM is present in the Golgi and cilia of C. reinhardtii.
source: Using an antibody recognizing the cytosolic domain of CrPAM, we found that this enzyme is present in the Golgi and cilia (aka flagella).
evidence: This finding is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PAM is present in motile and primary cilia of mammalian cells (tracheal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, spermatozoa).
source: PAM was also observed in motile and primary cilia of mammalian cells (tracheal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, spermatozoa) (Kumar et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016b.

claim: In C. reinhardtii cilia, PAM activity displayed a strong biochemical association with the axonemal superstructure.
source: Furthermore, in C. reinhardtii cilia, PAM activity displayed an unexpected, strong biochemical association with the axonemal superstructure (Kumar et al., 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016b and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: PAM has a novel and highly conserved signaling or sensory function in eukaryotic cilia.
source: Together, these observations in multiple cell types suggested that PAM has a novel and highly conserved signaling or sensory function in eukaryotic cilia.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the localization data.

claim: Seven CrPAM knockdown transformants and two empty vector control transformants were chosen for phenotypic analysis.
source: CrPAM protein expression was assessed by western blot analysis of whole cell lysates; seven transformants and two empty vector control transformants were chosen for further phenotypic analysis.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: All seven CrPAM knockdown strains were immotile and lacked cilia.
source: Phase-contrast microscopy revealed that all seven knockdown strains were immotile and lacked cilia.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy analysis.

claim: Lysates of PAM-amiRNA2 #3 and #8 strains contained reduced amounts of PAM protein.
source: Lysates of both strains contained reduced amounts of PAM protein (Figure 1B).
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 1B western blot.

claim: PHM and PAL activity was reduced in PAM-amiRNA2 #3 and #8 strains compared to empty vector transformed control strains.
source: Enzyme assays showed reduced levels of PHM and PAL activity in both strains (Figure 1C). Compared to empty vector transformed control strains, activity was reduced to about 30% and 10% in PAM-amiRNA2 #3 and #8, respectively.
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 1C enzyme activity assays.

claim: PAM activity was reduced to about 30% in PAM-amiRNA2 #3 strain.
source: Compared to empty vector transformed control strains, activity was reduced to about 30% and 10% in PAM-amiRNA2 #3 and #8, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantification of enzyme activity data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PAM activity was reduced to about 10% in PAM-amiRNA2 #8 strain.
source: Compared to empty vector transformed control strains, activity was reduced to about 30% and 10% in PAM-amiRNA2 #3 and #8, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantification of enzyme activity data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CrPAM staining is present in the cilium and Golgi of control cells.
source: Right panels show CrPAM staining in the cilium (inset) and Golgi, which is lost in knockdown cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D immunofluorescence images.

claim: CrPAM staining is lost in PAM knockdown cells.
source: Right panels show CrPAM staining in the cilium (inset) and Golgi, which is lost in knockdown cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D immunofluorescence images.

claim: Acetylated tubulin staining shows loss of cilia in PAM knockdown cells.
source: Acetylated tubulin staining shows loss of cilia; cortical microtubules are still visible in knockdown cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D immunofluorescence images.

claim: Cortical microtubules are still visible in PAM knockdown cells.
source: Acetylated tubulin staining shows loss of cilia; cortical microtubules are still visible in knockdown cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D immunofluorescence images.

claim: Most control cells had two cilia that were each ~10 µm in length.
source: Most control cells had two cilia that were each ~10 µm in length.
evidence: This is a quantification from scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cilia were never observed on cells of PAM knockdown strains by scanning electron microscopy.
source: In contrast, cilia were never observed on cells of either knockdown strain; only short ciliary stubs were visible (inset in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E scanning electron microscopy images.

claim: Only short ciliary stubs were visible on PAM knockdown cells.
source: In contrast, cilia were never observed on cells of either knockdown strain; only short ciliary stubs were visible (inset in Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E scanning electron microscopy images.

claim: PAM-amiRNA cells appeared morphologically normal in size and shape.
source: PAM-amiRNA cells otherwise appeared morphologically normal in size and shape (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from scanning electron microscopy images shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Both PAM knockdown strains grew at the same rate as controls in both acetate-containing and minimal media.
source: Both knockdown strains grew at the same rate as controls in both acetate-containing and minimal media (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A growth curves.

claim: Growth under both photoautotrophic and photoheterotrophic conditions was unaltered in PAM-amiRNA cells.
source: This clearly indicates that the PAM-amiRNA cells are generally healthy and do not exhibit major metabolic defects in chloroplast or mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the growth data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PAM-amiRNA cells do not exhibit major metabolic defects in chloroplast or mitochondrial function.
source: This clearly indicates that the PAM-amiRNA cells are generally healthy and do not exhibit major metabolic defects in chloroplast or mitochondrial function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the normal growth rates under photoautotrophic and photoheterotrophic conditions.

claim: The period of the contractile vacuole cycle was indistinguishable in knockdown and control strains.
source: The period of the contractile vacuole cycle, which relies on vesicular trafficking, was indistinguishable in knockdown and control strains grown under standard culture conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: Another amiRNA (amiRNA1) targeting a different region of the PAM gene also led to reduction of PAM activity and defective ciliogenesis.
source: To confirm the specificity of the knockdown, we used another amiRNA (amiRNA1) targeting a different region of the PAM gene (Figure 1A), and found that this also lead to reduction of PAM activity and defective ciliogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Table 1.

claim: The observed phenotypes are not the result of off-target effects from any given amiRNA.
source: Thus, the observed phenotypes are not the result of off-target effects from any given amiRNA.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that two different amiRNAs targeting different regions of the PAM gene produced similar phenotypes.

claim: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM is not required for enzyme activity.
source: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM is not required for enzyme activity, but controls its endocytic trafficking, and acts as a hub for various cytosolic protein interactions (Milgram et al., 1993; Prigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Milgram et al., 1993 and Prigge et al., 1997.

claim: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM controls its endocytic trafficking.
source: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM is not required for enzyme activity, but controls its endocytic trafficking, and acts as a hub for various cytosolic protein interactions (Milgram et al., 1993; Prigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Milgram et al., 1993 and Prigge et al., 1997.

claim: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM acts as a hub for various cytosolic protein interactions.
source: The cytosolic domain of mammalian PAM is not required for enzyme activity, but controls its endocytic trafficking, and acts as a hub for various cytosolic protein interactions (Milgram et al., 1993; Prigge et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Milgram et al., 1993 and Prigge et al., 1997.

claim: The CrPAM-ΔCD mutant encoded a protein lacking the final 73 residues of the 101-residue cytosolic domain of CrPAM.
source: The C. reinhardtii insertional mutant obtained (CrPAM-ΔCD) encoded a protein lacking the final 73 residues of the 101-residue cytosolic domain of CrPAM; the first 28 residues of the cytosolic domain were followed by an 18-amino acid sequence derived from the insertion cassette (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A schematic.

claim: Lysates prepared from the CrPAM-ΔCD mutant strain exhibited significantly more PHM and PAL enzyme activity than the control CC4533 strain.
source: Lysates prepared from the CrPAM-ΔCD mutant strain exhibited significantly more PHM and PAL enzyme activity than the control CC4533 strain (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B enzyme activity assays.

claim: Antibody specific for the cytosolic domain of CrPAM failed to detect any cross-reactive protein in CrPAM-ΔCD lysates.
source: As expected, antibody specific for the cytosolic domain of CrPAM failed to detect any cross-reactive protein in CrPAM-ΔCD lysates.
evidence: This is an observation from western blot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Levels of CrPAM-ΔCD protein exceeded levels of CrPAM protein.
source: In agreement with the activity measurements, levels of CrPAM-ΔCD protein exceeded levels of CrPAM protein, perhaps reflecting its altered trafficking and turnover (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B,C western blot and enzyme activity data.

claim: The CrPAM-ΔCD cells were motile.
source: The CrPAM-ΔCD cells were motile, with cilia that were similar in length to control cells (9.4 ± 0.2 µm for CC4533 and 9.5 ± 0.2 µm for CrPAM-ΔCD cells; n > 80 for each strain) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D microscopy images.

claim: Cilia in CrPAM-ΔCD cells were similar in length to control cells.
source: The CrPAM-ΔCD cells were motile, with cilia that were similar in length to control cells (9.4 ± 0.2 µm for CC4533 and 9.5 ± 0.2 µm for CrPAM-ΔCD cells; n > 80 for each strain) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantification from microscopy measurements.

claim: Transmission electron microscopy revealed no apparent ultrastructural defects in the cilia of CrPAM-ΔCD cells.
source: Transmission electron microscopy revealed no apparent ultrastructural defects in the cilia of CrPAM-ΔCD cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: CrPAM does not require an intact C-terminus in order to support ciliogenesis.
source: The fact that CrPAM does not require an intact C-terminus in order to support ciliogenesis suggests that the catalytic cores may provide the essential ciliogenic factor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CrPAM-ΔCD cells have normal cilia.

claim: 4-phenyl-3-butenoic acid (PBA) is a mechanism-based PHM inhibitor.
source: To further examine this hypothesis, we tested whether C. reinhardtii PHM activity was inhibited by 4-phenyl-3-butenoic acid (PBA), a mechanism-based PHM inhibitor that has been used in vitro and in vivo (Bradbury et al., 1990; Driscoll et al., 2000; Katopodis and May, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bradbury et al., 1990; Driscoll et al., 2000; Katopodis and May, 1990.

claim: PBA did not affect the growth properties of C. reinhardtii.
source: PBA did not affect the growth properties of C. reinhardtii (Figure 2F), but did inhibit both mammalian and C. reinhardtii PHM activities (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F growth assay.

claim: PBA inhibited both mammalian and C. reinhardtii PHM activities.
source: PBA did not affect the growth properties of C. reinhardtii (Figure 2F), but did inhibit both mammalian and C. reinhardtii PHM activities (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G and H enzyme activity assays.

claim: When C. reinhardtii cells were deflagellated and allowed to regenerate cilia in the presence of PBA, ciliary regrowth was delayed.
source: When C. reinhardtii cells were deflagellated and allowed to regenerate cilia in the presence of PBA, ciliary regrowth was delayed, suggesting that PAM enzymatic activity is important for ciliogenesis (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2I ciliary regrowth assay.

claim: PAM enzymatic activity is important for ciliogenesis.
source: When C. reinhardtii cells were deflagellated and allowed to regenerate cilia in the presence of PBA, ciliary regrowth was delayed, suggesting that PAM enzymatic activity is important for ciliogenesis (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is an inference based on the PBA inhibitor experiment shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Neocuproine is a highly selective copper chelator.
source: To further confirm this result, we deflagellated cells treated with neocuproine, a highly selective copper chelator (Mendelsohn et al., 2006) as the PHM-mediated hydroxylation reaction absolutely requires this metal.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mendelsohn et al., 2006.

claim: The PHM-mediated hydroxylation reaction absolutely requires copper.
source: To further confirm this result, we deflagellated cells treated with neocuproine, a highly selective copper chelator (Mendelsohn et al., 2006) as the PHM-mediated hydroxylation reaction absolutely requires this metal.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PHM enzymatic mechanism.

claim: Neocuproine treatment delayed reformation of ~9.5 μm cilia by 20–30 mins.
source: Neocuproine treatment delayed reformation of ~9.5 μm cilia by 20–30 mins (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2J ciliary regrowth assay.

claim: Analysis of the PAM-ΔCD strain and the enzyme inhibitor studies support a role for PAM activity in ciliogenesis.
source: Together, analysis of the PAM-ΔCD strain and the enzyme inhibitor studies support a role for PAM activity in ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data from the PAM-ΔCD strain and inhibitor experiments.

claim: The basal bodies appeared normal in PAM knockdown cells.
source: Compared to the normal ciliary morphology observed in longitudinal sections of control cells (Figure 3A), we observed only short ciliary stubs in PAM knockdown cells. The basal bodies appeared normal; however, we were unable to observe normal axonemal structures extending beyond the transition zone in these cells (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-E transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Normal axonemal structures extending beyond the transition zone were not observed in PAM knockdown cells.
source: The basal bodies appeared normal; however, we were unable to observe normal axonemal structures extending beyond the transition zone in these cells (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-E transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Most of the short ciliary stubs seen in PAM knockdown cells contained accumulations of electron dense material.
source: Most of the short ciliary stubs seen in PAM knockdown cells contained accumulations of electron dense material; some also had randomly oriented fragments of microtubules (arrows in Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and C transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Some ciliary stubs in PAM knockdown cells had randomly oriented fragments of microtubules.
source: Most of the short ciliary stubs seen in PAM knockdown cells contained accumulations of electron dense material; some also had randomly oriented fragments of microtubules (arrows in Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and C transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Y linkers were readily apparent in longitudinal sections through the transition zone of control cilia.
source: Wedge-shaped Y linkers, which connect the microtubules to the membrane and regulate protein entry into the cilium (arrowheads in Figure 3A), were readily apparent in longitudinal sections through the transition zone of control cilia.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A transmission electron microscopy image.

claim: Y linkers were not found in the transition zones of PAM knockdown cells.
source: However, we were unable to find Y linkers in the transition zones of PAM knockdown cells (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: The phenotypes observed in the PAM knockdown cells closely mirrored those previously reported for several IFT and transition zone mutants.
source: Overall, the phenotypes observed in the PAM knockdown cells closely mirrored those previously reported for several IFT and transition zone mutants (Craige et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2007; Pazour et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Craige et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2007; Pazour et al., 2000.

claim: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a bifunctional PAM protein with a transmembrane domain and cytosolic domain.
source: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a bifunctional PAM protein with a transmembrane domain and cytosolic domain, a soluble PHM protein and a soluble PAL protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A schematic.

claim: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a soluble PHM protein.
source: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a bifunctional PAM protein with a transmembrane domain and cytosolic domain, a soluble PHM protein and a soluble PAL protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A schematic.

claim: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a soluble PAL protein.
source: The S. mediterranea genome encodes a bifunctional PAM protein with a transmembrane domain and cytosolic domain, a soluble PHM protein and a soluble PAL protein (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A schematic.

claim: Reductions in PAM and/or PHM mRNA were observed in animals fed with Smed-phm(RNAi) or Smed-pam(RNAi) or a mixture of both.
source: RNA abundance was monitored using RT-PCR. Reductions in PAM and/or PHM mRNA were observed as expected in animals fed with Smed-phm(RNAi) or Smed-pam(RNAi) or a mixture of both; actin and outer arm dynein IC2 mRNA levels were unaltered (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B RT-PCR analysis.

claim: Actin and outer arm dynein IC2 mRNA levels were unaltered in planaria RNAi experiments.
source: Reductions in PAM and/or PHM mRNA were observed as expected in animals fed with Smed-phm(RNAi) or Smed-pam(RNAi) or a mixture of both; actin and outer arm dynein IC2 mRNA levels were unaltered (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B RT-PCR analysis.

claim: PHM activity was reduced to ~40% in Smed-pam(RNAi) and Smed-phm(RNAi) animals.
source: PHM activity was reduced to ~40% in Smed-pam(RNAi) and Smed-phm(RNAi) animals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C enzyme activity assays.

claim: Knockdown of both Smed-pam and Smed-phm reduced PHM specific activity to less than 10% of control.
source: Knockdown of both Smed-pam and Smed-phm reduced PHM specific activity to less than 10% of control.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C enzyme activity assays.

claim: PAL activity was reduced in lysates prepared from Smed-pam and the double knockdown animals, but not in Smed-phm(RNAi) planaria.
source: As expected, PAL activity was reduced in lysates prepared from Smed-pam and the double knockdown animals, but not in Smed-phm(RNAi) planaria.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C enzyme activity assays.

claim: Most of the PAL enzyme activity in planaria was derived from the bifunctional enzyme.
source: Our results also show that most of the PAL enzyme activity was derived from the bifunctional enzyme (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the enzyme activity data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A greater percentage of the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) animals were immotile compared to controls.
source: Compared to the controls, a greater percentage of the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) animals were immotile (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: Gliding velocity for Smed-pam(RNAi) planaria was comparable to L4440 controls (≈0.7 mm/s).
source: Interestingly, gliding velocity for Smed-pam(RNAi) planaria was comparable to L4440 controls (≈0.7 mm/s), while gliding velocities for Smed-phm(RNAi) and the double knockdown animals were lower (≈0.4 mm/s) (Figure 4E and Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Table 2.

claim: Gliding velocities for Smed-phm(RNAi) and the double knockdown animals were lower (≈0.4 mm/s).
source: Interestingly, gliding velocity for Smed-pam(RNAi) planaria was comparable to L4440 controls (≈0.7 mm/s), while gliding velocities for Smed-phm(RNAi) and the double knockdown animals were lower (≈0.4 mm/s) (Figure 4E and Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Table 2.

claim: Planarians completely devoid of cilia move at velocities similar to those of the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) animals by using muscular contractions.
source: Planarians completely devoid of cilia move at velocities similar to those of the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) animals by using muscular contractions to propel their bodies forward (Rompolas et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2010.

claim: PHM activity is necessary for normal motility behavior in planarians.
source: These results suggested that PHM activity was necessary for normal motility behavior in planarians.
evidence: This is an inference based on the motility data shown in Figure 4E and Table 2.

claim: Cilia in L4440 control planaria had a CBF of ≈ 26 Hz.
source: As observed previously, cilia in L4440 control animals had a CBF of ≈ 26 Hz (Rompolas et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 and supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2010.

claim: In PHM and double knockdown planaria, CBF was decreased to ≈ 18 Hz and ≈ 17 Hz, respectively.
source: In PHM and double knockdown animals, CBF was decreased to ≈ 18 Hz and ≈ 17 Hz, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: The CBF in the Smed-pam(RNAi) knockdown animals was ≈ 30 Hz.
source: The CBF in the Smed-pam(RNAi) knockdown animals was ≈ 30 Hz, consistent with the normal gliding velocity measured for this experimental group (Figure 4E and Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: The waveform of cilia in the double knockdown planaria appeared to be dramatically different from control animals.
source: The waveform of cilia in the double knockdown animals appeared to be dramatically different from control animals, with restricted motion compared to the highly coordinated smooth waveform of control cilia (Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Video 2.

claim: Knockdown of both PHM and PAM in planaria resulted in a severe reduction in ciliary density.
source: Scanning electron microscopy revealed dense, tightly packed cilia covering the entire ventral surface of L4440 control animals (Figure 5A). In stark contrast, knockdown of both PHM and PAM resulted in a severe reduction in ciliary density; planarian cilia undergo constant remodeling and ciliary loss is due to the failure of this process (Rompolas et al., 2010) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A scanning electron microscopy images.

claim: Planarian cilia undergo constant remodeling.
source: In stark contrast, knockdown of both PHM and PAM resulted in a severe reduction in ciliary density; planarian cilia undergo constant remodeling and ciliary loss is due to the failure of this process (Rompolas et al., 2010) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2010.

claim: Ciliary loss in planaria is due to the failure of the remodeling process.
source: In stark contrast, knockdown of both PHM and PAM resulted in a severe reduction in ciliary density; planarian cilia undergo constant remodeling and ciliary loss is due to the failure of this process (Rompolas et al., 2010) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rompolas et al., 2010.

claim: Flatworms receiving only Smed-phm(RNAi) or Smed-pam(RNAi) displayed intermediate phenotypes.
source: Flatworms receiving only Smed-phm(RNAi) or Smed-pam(RNAi) displayed intermediate phenotypes.
evidence: This is an observation from scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ciliary length was very heterogeneous in the RNAi-fed planaria.
source: Ciliary length was very heterogeneous in the RNAi-fed animals - short cilia were interspersed with cilia of normal length, presumably due to variations in the ciliary remodeling process (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A scanning electron microscopy images.

claim: Loss of PHM activity alone resulted in a ciliogenesis defect in planaria.
source: As loss of PHM activity alone resulted in a ciliogenesis defect in planaria, these results further support a role for amidating activity in this process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the planaria RNAi data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Cilia with a normal 9 + 2 axonemal structure, containing outer and inner dynein arms, were observed in all planaria samples.
source: Transmission electron microscopy also revealed pleomorphic defects resulting from the loss of PHM or both PHM and PAM in RNAi-fed planarians. In cross-sections, cilia with a normal 9 + 2 axonemal structure, containing outer and inner dynein arms, were observed in all samples (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B-D transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: In the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) planaria samples, the doublet microtubule organization was occasionally altered.
source: Occasionally, in the Smed-phm(RNAi) and Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) samples, the doublet microtubule organization was altered; singlet microtubules were sometimes observed along with doublet microtubules and in other cases the number of microtubules was aberrant (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E,F transmission electron microscopy images.

claim: Aberrant axonemal structures in planaria are likely a secondary feature of defective remodeling.
source: These aberrant axonemal structures are likely a secondary feature of defective remodeling; they may represent cilia in the process of failing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the electron microscopy data.

claim: In Smed-L4440 control samples, basal bodies docked at the plasma membrane and cilia extended outward.
source: In Smed-L4440 control samples, basal bodies docked at the plasma membrane and cilia extended outward (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G transmission electron microscopy image.

claim: Some docked basal bodies in Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) samples had no cilia emanating from them.
source: Although similar structures were present in the Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) sections, some docked basal bodies had no cilia emanating from them (arrowhead, Figure 5H and Table 3); there was an approximately 30% reduction in the density of docked basal bodies in the RNAi animals (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H and Table 3.

claim: There was an approximately 30% reduction in the density of docked basal bodies in the Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) planaria.
source: Although similar structures were present in the Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) sections, some docked basal bodies had no cilia emanating from them (arrowhead, Figure 5H and Table 3); there was an approximately 30% reduction in the density of docked basal bodies in the RNAi animals (Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3.

claim: Morphologically normal axonemes were repeatedly observed in the cytoplasm of the double knockdown planaria.
source: Furthermore, we repeatedly noticed the striking occurrence of morphologically normal axonemes in the cytoplasm of the double knockdown animals (n = 29 in 94 μm of epithelial length examined for Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) vs n = 0 in 145 μm of epithelial length examined for control animals); these cytoplasmic axonemes were not surrounded by a membrane and were never observed in any of the other RNAi or L4440 control samples (Figure 5H–K and Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H-K and Table 3.

claim: Cytoplasmic axonemes in double knockdown planaria were not surrounded by a membrane.
source: Furthermore, we repeatedly noticed the striking occurrence of morphologically normal axonemes in the cytoplasm of the double knockdown animals (n = 29 in 94 μm of epithelial length examined for Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) vs n = 0 in 145 μm of epithelial length examined for control animals); these cytoplasmic axonemes were not surrounded by a membrane and were never observed in any of the other RNAi or L4440 control samples (Figure 5H–K and Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H-K and Table 3.

claim: Cytoplasmic axonemes were never observed in any of the other RNAi or L4440 control planaria samples.
source: Furthermore, we repeatedly noticed the striking occurrence of morphologically normal axonemes in the cytoplasm of the double knockdown animals (n = 29 in 94 μm of epithelial length examined for Smed-phm+pam(RNAi) vs n = 0 in 145 μm of epithelial length examined for control animals); these cytoplasmic axonemes were not surrounded by a membrane and were never observed in any of the other RNAi or L4440 control samples (Figure 5H–K and Table 3).
evidence: This is shown in Table 3.

claim: Mislocalized cytosolic axonemes in planaria appeared to have a normal 9 + 2 ultrastructure containing inner and outer dynein arms.
source: Intriguingly, these mislocalized cytosolic axonemes appeared to have a normal 9 + 2 ultrastructure containing inner and outer dynein arms (Figure 5K) and were in general oriented along the long axis of the animal with the axonemal distal tip towards the head.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5K transmission electron microscopy image.

claim: Cytosolic axonemes in planaria were in general oriented along the long axis of the animal with the axonemal distal tip towards the head.
source: Intriguingly, these mislocalized cytosolic axonemes appeared to have a normal 9 + 2 ultrastructure containing inner and outer dynein arms (Figure 5K) and were in general oriented along the long axis of the animal with the axonemal distal tip towards the head.
evidence: This is an observation from transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The ectopic localization of axonemes in the cytoplasm arising due to PAM deficiency suggests a defect in basal body docking and/or ciliary membrane trafficking.
source: The ectopic localization of axonemes in the cytoplasm arising due to PAM deficiency suggests a defect in basal body docking and/or ciliary membrane trafficking.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of cytoplasmic axonemes in planaria.

claim: Deletion of the Pam gene in mice results in embryonic lethality.
source: Deletion of the Pam gene in mice results in embryonic lethality; embryos display massive pericardial edema and die by E14.5-E15.5 (Czyzyk et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Czyzyk et al., 2005.

claim: Pam-/- mouse embryos display massive pericardial edema and die by E14.5-E15.5.
source: Deletion of the Pam gene in mice results in embryonic lethality; embryos display massive pericardial edema and die by E14.5-E15.5 (Czyzyk et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Czyzyk et al., 2005.

claim: Zebrafish and rodent ciliary mutants display a similar edematous phenotype to Pam-/- mice.
source: The cause and source of this edema in Pam-/- embryos is unclear, but zebrafish and rodent ciliary mutants display a similar edematous phenotype (Gorivodsky et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gorivodsky et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016b; Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: Primary cilia emerge from ciliary pockets in epithelial cells in the lateral ventricular surface of wild type mouse embryos.
source: As expected, we observed primary cilia emerging from ciliary pockets in epithelial cells in the lateral ventricular surface of wild type embryos.
evidence: This is an observation from scanning electron microscopy shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cilia were present in Pam-/- neuroepithelial cells, although their morphology differed from cilia in wild-type animals.
source: Cilia were also present in Pam-/- neuroepithelial cells, although their morphology differed from cilia in wild-type animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A scanning electron microscopy images.

claim: Ciliary density was unaffected in the Pam-/- mouse embryos.
source: Ciliary density was unaffected in the Pam-/- embryos (Figure 6B), but the cilia in these embryos were significantly shorter than controls (Figure 6C) (0.66 ± 0.01 μm in WT vs. 0.55 ± 0.01 μm in Pam-/- animals; n > 500).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Cilia in Pam-/- mouse embryos were significantly shorter than controls.
source: Ciliary density was unaffected in the Pam-/- embryos (Figure 6B), but the cilia in these embryos were significantly shorter than controls (Figure 6C) (0.66 ± 0.01 μm in WT vs. 0.55 ± 0.01 μm in Pam-/- animals; n > 500).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Cilia measured 0.51 ± 0.04 µm (n = 69) in Pam-/- vs. 0.90 ± 0.08 µm (n = 45) in WT mouse embryos by transmission electron microscopy.
source: Since the longer control cilia were often bent, we also used transmission electron microscopy to confirm the presence of stumpy cilia in the PAM-/- animals; cilia measured 0.51 ± 0.04 µm (n = 69) in Pam-/- vs. 0.90 ± 0.08 µm (n = 45) in WT (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: PAM has a key and highly conserved role in ciliogenesis.
source: These combined data from three very different model organisms clearly reveal that PAM has a key and highly conserved role in ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from C. reinhardtii, planaria, and mice.

claim: Total α-tubulin levels were unaltered in PAM amiRNA cells.
source: Although total α-tubulin levels were unaltered in PAM amiRNA cells, levels of acetylated tubulin and poly-glutamylated tubulin, modified forms present in cilia, were both significantly lower compared to control cell lysates, consistent with the loss of cilia (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B western blot analysis.

claim: Levels of acetylated tubulin and poly-glutamylated tubulin were both significantly lower in PAM amiRNA cells compared to control cell lysates.
source: Although total α-tubulin levels were unaltered in PAM amiRNA cells, levels of acetylated tubulin and poly-glutamylated tubulin, modified forms present in cilia, were both significantly lower compared to control cell lysates, consistent with the loss of cilia (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A,B western blot analysis.

claim: Arf1 levels were unchanged in lysates of PAM knockdown cells.
source: Arf1 levels were unchanged in lysates of PAM knockdown cells, while clathrin levels were increased compared to control lysates (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C,D western blot analysis.

claim: Clathrin levels were increased in PAM knockdown cells compared to control lysates.
source: Arf1 levels were unchanged in lysates of PAM knockdown cells, while clathrin levels were increased compared to control lysates (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C,D western blot analysis.

claim: Certain membrane trafficking processes involving clathrin were affected in PAM amiRNA cells.
source: This result suggested that certain membrane trafficking processes involving clathrin were affected in PAM amiRNA cells, while the contractile vacuole cycle, another membrane trafficking process, was unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased clathrin levels and normal contractile vacuole function.

claim: Both PAM amiRNA strains contained greatly increased amounts of CEP290 and NPHP4 compared to controls.
source: Levels of two transition zone components, CEP290 and NPHP4 (Awata et al., 2014) were monitored. Both PAM amiRNA strains contained greatly increased amounts of CEP290 and NPHP4 compared to controls (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F,G western blot analysis.

claim: C. reinhardtii CEP290 null mutants have short stumpy cilia.
source: CEP290 is a component of the Y linkers and C. reinhardtii CEP290 null mutants have short stumpy cilia (Craige et al., 2010) much like those observed in the PAM knockdown cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Craige et al., 2010.

claim: NPHP4 is an essential part of the barrier at the ciliary base.
source: NPHP4, a more distal component of the transition zone, is an essential part of the barrier at the ciliary base (Awata et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Awata et al., 2014.

claim: Cells may respond to an assembly defect caused by reduced levels of CrPAM with a compensatory up-regulation of specific transition zone proteins.
source: It is possible that cells respond to an assembly defect caused by the reduced levels of CrPAM with a compensatory up-regulation of specific transition zone proteins.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the increased CEP290 and NPHP4 protein levels.

claim: RNA-seq analysis revealed that the transcript abundance of CEP290 and NPHP4 was unchanged in PAM amiRNA cells.
source: Interestingly, RNA-seq analysis revealed that the transcript abundance of these transition zone components was unchanged in PAM amiRNA cells (Supplementary file 1), pointing to a post-transcriptional regulatory response that alters CEP290 and NPHP4 protein levels in the absence of PAM.
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: A post-transcriptional regulatory response alters CEP290 and NPHP4 protein levels in the absence of PAM.
source: Interestingly, RNA-seq analysis revealed that the transcript abundance of these transition zone components was unchanged in PAM amiRNA cells (Supplementary file 1), pointing to a post-transcriptional regulatory response that alters CEP290 and NPHP4 protein levels in the absence of PAM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the discrepancy between mRNA and protein levels.

claim: Brefeldin A treatment for 3 hr decreased ciliary length in control C. reinhardtii cells.
source: To assess whether Golgi disruption caused the same effects on tubulin post-translational modification and transition zone protein expression as observed in the PAM-amiRNA strain, we treated control ciliated cells with brefeldin A (BFA) for 3 hr and observed the expected decrease in ciliary length (Dentler, 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the brefeldin A experiment, supported by a citation to Dentler, 2013.

claim: The levels of acetylated and glutamylated tubulin were decreased in both PAM-amiRNA and brefeldin A-treated cells.
source: The levels of acetylated and glutamylated tubulin were decreased in both PAM-amiRNA and brefeldin A-treated cells, consistent with loss of cilia.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Enhanced levels of the transition zone protein NPHP4 were not observed following brefeldin A treatment.
source: However, enhanced levels of the transition zone protein NPHP4 were not observed following brefeldin A treatment, indicating that this response is specific to PAM deficiency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Brefeldin A treatment increased Arf1 levels, a response not observed in the PAM-amiRNA strains.
source: Brefeldin A treatment increased Arf1 levels, a response not observed in the PAM-amiRNA strains.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PAM knockdown phenotype is distinct from a generalized Golgi dysfunction phenotype.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the PAM knockdown phenotype is distinct from a generalized Golgi dysfunction phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of PAM knockdown and brefeldin A treatment effects.

claim: In control cells, punctate CEP290 staining was apparent at the base of each cilium.
source: In control cells, punctate CEP290 staining was apparent at the base of each cilium (Figure 7H upper panels, enlargements on right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H immunofluorescence images.

claim: In PAM amiRNA cells, the localization pattern of CEP290 remained unchanged in the basal body region.
source: In PAM amiRNA cells, the localization pattern of CEP290 remained unchanged in the basal body region, which was identified by using antiserum to acetylated tubulin to locate the anterior portion of the cortical microtubules (Figure 7H, lower panels).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H immunofluorescence images.

claim: Additional CEP290 immunoreactive puncta were visible in the cell body of PAM amiRNA cells.
source: However, additional CEP290 immunoreactive puncta were visible in the cell body (Figure 7H, arrows).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7H immunofluorescence images.

claim: Alterations in the levels of specific transition zone and membrane trafficking proteins may contribute to the defects observed in PAM amiRNA C. reinhardtii cells.
source: These alterations in the levels of specific transition zone and membrane trafficking proteins, which are critical components of the ciliary assembly machinery, may contribute to the defects observed in PAM amiRNA C. reinhardtii cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the protein level changes observed.

claim: RNA-seq analysis and immunoblotting showed that the levels of core anterograde IFT-B components, such as IFT46 and IFT72/74, were unaltered in PAM knockdown cells.
source: Both RNA-seq analysis and immunoblotting showed that the levels of core anterograde IFT-B components, such as IFT46 and IFT72/74, were unaltered in PAM knockdown cells (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1 and Figure 8A,B.

claim: IFT81 levels were increased in CrPAM amiRNA strain #8 but not in strain #3.
source: IFT81 levels were increased in CrPAM amiRNA strain #8 but not in strain #3 (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A,B western blot analysis.

claim: IFT81 levels may be sensitive only to a severe deficiency of CrPAM.
source: Since, strain #8 had lower amounts of CrPAM than strain #3 (Figure 7A,B), IFT81 levels may be sensitive only to a severe deficiency of CrPAM.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between PAM levels and IFT81 levels.

claim: IFT proteins normally display a punctate localization in the cilium and accumulate at its base, close to the basal body.
source: IFT proteins normally display a punctate localization in the cilium and accumulate at its base, close to the basal body.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about IFT protein localization.

claim: In PAM amiRNA cells, IFT72/74 staining was observed in the ciliary stubs and staining in the peri-basal body region was reduced.
source: In PAM amiRNA cells, IFT72/74 staining was observed in the ciliary stubs (Figure 8C, insets) and staining in the peri-basal body region was reduced.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8C immunofluorescence images.

claim: In PAM amiRNA cells, both IFT46 and IFT81 were mostly located in the short ciliary stubs and the amount in the basal body region was reduced.
source: In the PAM amiRNA cells, both IFT components were mostly located in the short ciliary stubs and the amount in the basal body region was reduced (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8D immunofluorescence images.

claim: The abnormal accumulation of IFT components in the ciliary stubs may contribute to the increase in electron-dense amorphous material observed by electron microscopy.
source: The abnormal accumulation of IFT components in the ciliary stubs may contribute to the increase in electron-dense amorphous material observed by electron microscopy (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation linking the IFT accumulation to the electron microscopy observations.

claim: Lysates of PAM amiRNA strains contained increased amounts of IFT-A component IFT139 compared to control cell lysates.
source: Strikingly, lysates of PAM amiRNA strains contained increased amounts of IFT-A component IFT139 compared to control cell lysates (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E,F western blot analysis.

claim: Loss of IFT 139 in C. elegans leads to formation of abnormal, short cilia.
source: In C. elegans, loss of IFT 139 leads to formation of abnormal, short cilia (Niwa, 2016), and mutations in the human gene encoding IFT139 (TTC21B) have been linked to nephronophthisis and thoracic dystrophy (Davis et al., 2011; Huynh Cong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Niwa, 2016; Davis et al., 2011; Huynh Cong et al., 2014.

claim: Mutations in the human gene encoding IFT139 (TTC21B) have been linked to nephronophthisis and thoracic dystrophy.
source: In C. elegans, loss of IFT 139 leads to formation of abnormal, short cilia (Niwa, 2016), and mutations in the human gene encoding IFT139 (TTC21B) have been linked to nephronophthisis and thoracic dystrophy (Davis et al., 2011; Huynh Cong et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Davis et al., 2011; Huynh Cong et al., 2014.

claim: Levels of axonemal outer arm dynein intermediate chain (IC2) were unchanged in PAM amiRNA cell lysates.
source: Levels of axonemal outer arm dynein intermediate chain (IC2) were unchanged in PAM amiRNA cell lysates (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8E,F western blot analysis.

claim: Changes in PAM levels affect specific components of the IFT machinery.
source: Thus, changes in PAM levels affect specific components of the IFT machinery.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the selective changes in IFT protein levels.

claim: The compensatory increase in IFT139 occurs post-transcriptionally.
source: This compensatory increase occurs post-transcriptionally (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: CrPAM is largely localized to the Golgi region.
source: Like rat PAM, CrPAM is largely localized to the Golgi region (Kumar et al., 2016b); the membrane proteins needed by the growing cilium are provided by the Golgi.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kumar et al., 2016b.

claim: The membrane proteins needed by the growing cilium are provided by the Golgi.
source: Like rat PAM, CrPAM is largely localized to the Golgi region (Kumar et al., 2016b); the membrane proteins needed by the growing cilium are provided by the Golgi.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about ciliary membrane protein supply.

claim: The area occupied by the Golgi, number of cisternae and Golgi width were not significantly different in PAM amiRNA cells.
source: The area occupied by the Golgi, number of cisternae and Golgi width were not significantly different in PAM amiRNA cells (Figure 9B,C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9B,C,D quantifications.

claim: A significant difference in Golgi curvature was observed in PAM amiRNA cells.
source: However, a significant difference in Golgi curvature was observed (Figure 9E); Golgi stacks in the knockdown cells were more concave.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9E quantification.

claim: Golgi stacks in the PAM knockdown cells were more concave.
source: However, a significant difference in Golgi curvature was observed (Figure 9E); Golgi stacks in the knockdown cells were more concave.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9E quantification.

claim: Starch grains accumulate when Golgi function is inhibited.
source: Starch grains, which are present in the chloroplast, accumulate when Golgi function is inhibited (Hummel et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hummel et al., 2010.

claim: Starch grains occupied a larger fraction of the cell area in PAM knockdown cells compared to control cells.
source: Quantification revealed that starch grains occupied a larger fraction of the cell area in PAM knockdown cells compared to control cells; cell size did not differ (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B,C quantifications.

claim: Cell size did not differ between PAM knockdown and control cells.
source: Quantification revealed that starch grains occupied a larger fraction of the cell area in PAM knockdown cells compared to control cells; cell size did not differ (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10B,C quantifications.

claim: No significant difference in starch content was found between the PAM knockdown and control cells.
source: To determine whether this morphological change in starch grains correlated with an increase in starch content in the PAM amiRNA cells, we measured starch levels enzymatically and found no significant difference between the knockdown and control cells.
evidence: This is a result from enzymatic starch measurements.

claim: Enlarged starch grains without a concomitant increase in starch levels were previously noted in vacuolar membrane protein-1 (VMP1) knockdown strains.
source: Enlarged starch grains without a concomitant increase in starch levels were previously noted in vacuolar membrane protein-1 (VMP1) knockdown strains, which also displayed abnormal Golgi morphology (Tenenboim et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tenenboim et al., 2014.

claim: The results suggest an impact of PAM knockdown on Golgi function.
source: These results suggest an impact of PAM knockdown on Golgi function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Golgi morphology and starch grain changes.

claim: Iron deficiency conditions stimulate the secretion of FEA1 in C. reinhardtii.
source: Iron deficiency conditions (0.5 μM vs 20 μM Fe) stimulate the secretion of FEA1, an iron assimilation protein that is readily identifiable after electrophoretic separation of the spent medium, which in cell wall-less strains contains the secreted protein (Allen et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Allen et al., 2007.

claim: The 40 kDa FEA1 protein was readily detected in all strains under iron deficiency conditions.
source: As expected, the 40 kDa FEA1 protein was readily detected in all strains under iron deficiency conditions (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10D silver staining.

claim: Secretion of FEA1 was decreased in the PAM amiRNA strains compared to controls.
source: However, secretion of FEA1 was decreased in the PAM amiRNA strains compared to controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10D silver staining.

claim: There were striking differences in the secretome in PAM knockdown cells even under basal conditions.
source: Furthermore, there were striking differences in the secretome in PAM knockdown cells even under basal conditions (arrowheads and brackets, Figure 10C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10D silver staining.

claim: FEA1 transcript levels were two-fold higher in PAM amiRNA cells than in controls.
source: Surprisingly, FEA1 transcript levels were two-fold higher in PAM amiRNA cells than in controls, perhaps reflecting a compensatory measure (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Phosphate-deficient conditions stimulate secretion of alkaline phosphatase in C. reinhardtii.
source: We next cultured cells under phosphate-deficient conditions, which stimulates secretion of alkaline phosphatase (Quisel et al., 1996) or sulfate-deficient conditions, which stimulates secretion of arylsulfatase (de Hostos et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Quisel et al., 1996.

claim: Sulfate-deficient conditions stimulate secretion of arylsulfatase in C. reinhardtii.
source: We next cultured cells under phosphate-deficient conditions, which stimulates secretion of alkaline phosphatase (Quisel et al., 1996) or sulfate-deficient conditions, which stimulates secretion of arylsulfatase (de Hostos et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to de Hostos et al., 1988.

claim: Cellular alkaline phosphatase activity levels were indistinguishable in phosphate-deficient control and PAM amiRNA cells.
source: Cellular alkaline phosphatase activity levels were indistinguishable in phosphate-deficient control and PAM amiRNA cells; however, alkaline phosphatase secretion was greatly attenuated in PAM amiRNA strains compared to controls (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10E enzyme activity assays.

claim: Alkaline phosphatase secretion was greatly attenuated in PAM amiRNA strains compared to controls.
source: Cellular alkaline phosphatase activity levels were indistinguishable in phosphate-deficient control and PAM amiRNA cells; however, alkaline phosphatase secretion was greatly attenuated in PAM amiRNA strains compared to controls (Figure 10E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10E enzyme activity assays.

claim: Secretion of arylsulfatase by sulfate-deprived cells did not differ in PAM amiRNA and control cells.
source: In contrast, secretion of arylsulfatase by sulfate-deprived cells did not differ in PAM amiRNA and control cells (Figure 10F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 10F enzyme activity assays.

claim: The effect of PAM loss on secretion is selective and not a result of generalized Golgi dysfunction.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the effect of PAM loss on secretion is selective and not a result of generalized Golgi dysfunction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the selective effects on different secreted proteins.

claim: At least one of the ancestral and conserved roles of PAM is in ciliary assembly.
source: The evolutionarily widespread occurrence of the PAM gene and the results presented here suggest that at least one of the ancestral and conserved roles of PAM is in ciliary assembly.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the evolutionary conservation of PAM and its role in ciliogenesis across multiple organisms.

claim: Wildtype cells can regrow cilia even when PHM activity has been inhibited.
source: Our PBA and neocuproine studies indicate that wildtype cells can regrow cilia even when PHM activity has been inhibited.
evidence: This is an observation from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 2I,J.

claim: Cilia can regrow in the absence of enzymatically active PAM provided that all the necessary structures are already available.
source: Thus, it is possible that cilia can regrow in the absence of enzymatically active PAM provided that all the necessary structures (such as attached basal bodies, functional IFT machinery etc) are already available.

claim: Chlamydomonas stockpiles sufficient components to regenerate two approximately half-length cilia in the absence of additional protein synthesis.
